Saturn’s largest moon Titan is covered by a thick hazy atmosphere. However, if we can peer through the atmosphere, we find a surface composed of rock-hard water ice along with rolling dunes. There are also seas filled with liquid methane at Titan’s northern pole (Kraken, Ligeia, and Punga Mare). A smaller lake, Ontario Lacus, is found at the southern pole. Two large areas are situated along Titan’s equator. Shangri-La is a dark-colored lowland filled with flowing dunes. Xanadu is a light-colored plateau of ice with mounds and knolls extending above the ground (hummocky).

[![Image 12](https://i0.wp.com/www.fas37.org/wp/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/Titan_comp_ISSimage-pdf.jpg?resize=1024%2C683&ssl=1)](https://www.fas37.org/wp/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/Titan_comp_ISSimage.pdf)

Image Credit: NASA/JPL/Space Science Institute & USGA/IAU/NASA Gazetteer of Planetary Nomenclature

The most noticeable feature on Pluto’s surface is a heart shaped area that is filled with frozen nitrogen. Officially it is Tombaugh Regio (named after Pluto’s discoverer Clyde Tombaugh). The western portion is called Sputnik Planitia (named after the first artificial satellite). Another is a dark area filled with Tholins (organic gunk). It was initially (and unofficially) named Cthulhu Regio but is now officially Belton Regio (after astronomer Michael Belton).

Many of the surface features on Charon were unofficially named after science fiction references. These included Kirk, Spock, Sulu, and Uhura craters as well as Tardis Chasma and Gallifrey Macula. A dark area, filled with Tholins that carried over from Pluto, was initially referred to as Mordor Macula. However, most of these names have yet to be officially adopted and surface features now have more acceptable (mundane?) names.

# Planetary Names

**FAS Astronomers Blog, Volume 34, Number 5.**

From time to time, we witness a parade of planets across the evening sky. Well, almost. At times, some of the planets are very low in the horizon and difficult to see. But they’re still up there and officially we have eight planets in our solar system. Of course, there are also five official dwarf planets and if you travel farther out into the galaxy, there are over 6,000 known exoplanets.

###### Planets

Five of the official planets (Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn) were visible in the night sky and known in ancient times. According to[Geminus of Rhodes in _Elementa astronomiae_](https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/greek-astronomy/9F91981A18635032FD433FA8746F1361)(per Thomas Heath),[David Southworth](https://www.spacecentre.co.uk/news/space-now-blog/how-did-the-planets-get-their-names/), and[James Evans](https://global.oup.com/academic/product/the-history-and-practice-of-ancient-astronomy-9780195095395?cc=us&lang=en&), the Greeks named these planets after their characteristics: Stilbon (the gleaming star), Phosphorus (the light bringer or star of Aphrodite), Pyroeis (the fiery star), Phaethon (the bright star), and Phainon (the shining star). The Greeks then assigned gods from their mythology to watch over each planet. It is from here we get the Greek names: Hermes, Aphrodite, Ares, Zeus, and Cronus.

Evidently, as[Raymond Shubinski](https://www.astronomy.com/science/how-did-all-the-planets-with-their-moons-get-their-names/)and[John Burnet](https://books.google.com/books?id=7yUAmmqHHEgC&pg=PR4)point out, Venus proved to be a problem. It was initially thought to be two different planets, and they were named Phosphorus (morning) and Hesperus (evening). Eventually, folks figured out that they were one and the same and it became Aphrodite.

Much later, the Romans kept the same naming convention but converted the names to the Roman (Latin) equivalents: Mercurius, Venus, Mars, Iuppiter, and Saturnus. During the Renaissance, most scientific literature such as Newton’s Principia, were written in Latin, so the Latin names have remained with us, but with an English tweak to them: Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn.

The Earth has a different story. It is not named after either a Greek or Roman mythological god. Rather the name comes from old English (e.g., ertha) and old German (e.g., erde) – words meaning ground or soil. It is also not known who coined the term Earth, except that it has been used for a thousand years or more.

Everything was fine until William Herschel came along and found a new planet. This was the first one not known in antiquity, so it needed a name. For a time, it was simply referred to as planet Herschel. Herschel, who was born in Germany but emigrated to England, wanted to curry favor with King George III. He, therefore, proposed naming the new planet Georgium Sidus(Georgian Star). This didn’t sit too well with those outside of England. So, Johann Elbert Bode suggested it be named after the Greek god of the sky. Following Bode’s lead and to keep with tradition, Uranus – the Latin version of the Greek Ouranos was chosen. However, it is technically a Greek name and not the Roman equivalent, which evidently is Caelus (the god of the sky from Roman mythology). In the end, Uranus has stuck with us, although it is the only planet with a Greek rather than Roman name.

There is still a bit of a controversy over how to pronounce the name Uranus. You can find out more about this in a previous article,[What’s in the Name Uranus](https://www.fas37.org/wp/whats-in-the-name-uranus/). Although, I was recently asked, is this just an English issue or is there an issue with how to pronounce the name of this planet in other languages? The scientific community generally uses the English names, so I would think the controversy remains, however, I believe they mostly pronounce it “Ur-a-nus.” The name is also spelled Uranus in many languages including French and German, although the pronunciation may be different than the two found in English. Other languages, including Spanish and Portuguese, use Urano, which probably doesn’t have the same problem as the English pronunciation.

Neptune was discovered next. There is some controversy associated with its discovery. For more, see[The Discovery of Neptune](https://www.fas37.org/wp/the-discovery-of-neptune/). In the end, it was named after the Roman god of the sea – probably because of its blue color.

In 1930, Pluto was discovered by Clyde Tombaugh at the Lowell Observatory in Flagstaff, Arizona. It used to be a planet. Then, beginning in 2006, it wasn’t a planet anymore. You can find more about both the discovery and reclassification of Pluto in[Discovering Pluto](https://www.fas37.org/wp/discovering-pluto/)and[Reclassifying Pluto](https://www.fas37.org/wp/reclassifying-pluto/). After Pluto’s discovery, it needed a name. The folks at the Lowell Observatory had several in mind. However, a young British girl, Venetia Burney, had been reading about ancient mythology and thought the name Pluto, the Roman god of the underworld, was appropriate. Her suggestion made its way to the Lowell Observatory, and the newly discovered “planet” became Pluto. The Disney dog was evidently named later.

In any event, the planetary names still associate the planet with its characteristics.

*   **Mercury**is the swiftest planet and is named after the messenger god of travel and commerce.
*   **Venus**is a beautiful bright star in the sky and is named after the goddess of love and beauty.
*   **Mars**, with its reddish color, is named after the god of war.
*   **Jupiter**, the largest planet, is named after the king of gods.
*   **Saturn**, which slowly moves across the sky, is named after Cronus, the father of Zeus.
*   **Uranus**, with a pale blue color, is named for the Greek god of the sky and father of Cronus.
*   **Neptune**, with a blue color, is named after the god of the sea.
*   **Pluto**, deep in the far reaches of the Solar System, is named after the god of the underworld.

###### Dwarf Planets

As noted above there are five official dwarf planets and they needed names. We’ve covered Pluto because it used to be a planet. However, the other four have stories as well.

Ceres was discovered in 1801 by Giuseppe Piazzi at the same time as the discovery of the first few large asteroids. However, these new objects weren’t initially called asteroids, and for a time, they were considered full-fledged planets. They eventually found so many of them that they began referring to them as asteroids or minor planets. For more on this, see[Discovering Pluto](https://www.fas37.org/wp/discovering-pluto/).

Ceres is the only asteroid large enough to be round, so it was classified as a dwarf planet along with Pluto in 2006. After its initial discovery,Piazzi suggested the name Cerere Ferdinandea for the new object – after the Roman goddess of agriculture (Ceres) and King Ferdinand III of Sicily. But only the Ceres portion remained, and it became just Ceres.It is from this we get the name Cereal for our breakfast food.

Eris was initially nicknamed Xena after the TV warrior princess. Later, it was officially named after the Greek god of strife and discord. This was a fitting name because, at nearly the same size as Pluto, it was one of the reasons Pluto was reclassified. This brought strife and discord to the solar system as astronomers wrestled with the definition of a planet and the number of official planets.

Haumea and Makemake were discovered around the same time of Pluto’s reclassification and officially became dwarf planets a couple of years later. They were named by their discoverers based on separate creation myths. Haumea, initially nicknamed Santa, is a goddess in Hawaiian mythology. Makemake, initially nicknamed Easter Bunny, is the creator of humanity in the mythology of the Rapa Nui people from Easter Island in the south pacific.

###### Moons

Then came the moons – and there are many of them. So, it’s hard to keep up with them all, much less their names. Check with us at “[New Moons of the Solar System](https://www.fas37.org/wp/new-moons-for-the-solar-system/)” for an updated count (with reference to the[official list of moons from NASA](https://ssd.jpl.nasa.gov/sats/discovery.html)).

[![Image 4](https://i0.wp.com/www.fas37.org/wp/wp-content/uploads/2023/05/Moons-of-the-Solar-System.png?resize=1024%2C640&ssl=1)](https://i0.wp.com/www.fas37.org/wp/wp-content/uploads/2023/05/Moons-of-the-Solar-System.png?ssl=1)

Moons of the Solar System  
Image Credit: NASA/Johns Hopkins University Applied Physics Laboratory/Southwest Research Institute

The Earth’s moon was known back in antiquity – it is hard to miss it in the night sky. For a long time, it was the only moon (as far as we knew). The USGA notes that it has several names, but simply the Moon seems to be the choice in English.

Every civilization has had a name for the satellite of Earth that is known, in English, as the Moon. The Moon is known as Luna in Italian, Latin, and Spanish, as Lune in French, as Mond in German, and as Selene in Greek. (USGA “[Planet and Satellite Names and Discoverers](https://planetarynames.wr.usgs.gov/Page/Planets)”)

In 1610, when Galileo pointed his telescope up at the night sky, he noticed that Jupiter had four “stars” moving in its vicinity. After several nights, he concluded they were moons orbiting the planet. He needed to name these four moons. In many of his writings he simply referred to them as I, II, III, and IV. In addition, he proposed they be named the “Medicean Stars” in honor of his patron the Medici family. However, Simon Marius, who claimed to have observed the moons first, suggested names from Roman mythology and characters associated with Jupiter (Io, Europa, Ganymede, and Callisto). These names were also supported by Johannes Kepler but didn’t catch on for another couple hundred years. Today the four large moons of Jupiter are named as Marius proposed but are also called the Galilean moons after Galileo.

After his discovery of Uranus, William Herschel went on to find its two largest moons in 1787. Herschel, or possibly his son John, chose to name the moons Titania and Oberon – the queen and king of the fairies in Shakespeare’s _A Midsummers Night’s Dream_. At the suggestion of Herschel’s son John, the next two moons became Ariel and Umbriel from The _Rape of the Lock_ by Alexander Pope. The smaller Miranda is from _The Tempest_. As other moons were discovered they were also named after characters from Shakespeare.

Triton, the largest moon of Neptune (named after the Roman god of the sea and equivalent of the Greek Poseidon) is the Greek son of Poseidon. Other Neptunian moons have names associated with mythological characters of the sea or water. The moons of Pluto are all associated with the underworld (Charon, Styx, Nix, Kerberos, and Hydra).

Eris’ one moon Dysnomia is named after Eris’ daughter from Greek mythology. Haumea’s two moons were initially nicknamed Rudolph and Blitzen. They are now officially named after the daughters of Haumea. Hi’iaka is a goddess of the Big island of Hawaii and Namaka is the Hawaiian goddess of the sea. Makemake’s one moon is still referred to as MK1. I guess no one has gotten around to giving it a more formal name.

Today, moons are generally given names associated with their planet and from the mythology upon which the planet’s name is based. To keep everything in order, the International Astronomical Union’s Working Group for Planetary Nomenclature developed official[rules about how moons and surface features are named](https://planetarynames.wr.usgs.gov/Page/Planets).

###### Surface Features

Surface features are also managed by the[IAU’s working group](https://planetarynames.wr.usgs.gov/Nomenclature). There are too many to discuss them all here, but we can look at a few on [Mercury](https://planetarynames.wr.usgs.gov/Page/MERCURY/target),[Venus](https://planetarynames.wr.usgs.gov/Page/VENUS/target),[Mars](https://planetarynames.wr.usgs.gov/Page/MARS/target),[Ceres](https://planetarynames.wr.usgs.gov/Page/CERES/target),[Titan](https://planetarynames.wr.usgs.gov/Page/TITAN/target),[Pluto](https://planetarynames.wr.usgs.gov/Page/PLUTO/target)and its largest moon[Charon](https://planetarynames.wr.usgs.gov/Page/CHARON/target).

Mercury has a huge 900-mile-wide crater called Caloris Basin. It is likely an impact area that resulted from a collision with a large object some billions of years ago.

[![Image 5](https://i0.wp.com/www.fas37.org/wp/wp-content/uploads/2021/08/2266_PIA19216_1280.jpg?resize=1024%2C1006&ssl=1)](https://i0.wp.com/www.fas37.org/wp/wp-content/uploads/2021/08/2266_PIA19216_1280.jpg?ssl=1)

Caloris Basin  
Image Credit: NASA/Johns Hopkins University Applied Physics Laboratory/Carnegie Institution of Washington

Features on Venus are named for females with three exceptions. Maxwell Montes is the tallest mountain range and is named after James Clerk Maxwell. Alpha Regio and Beta Regio are two highland areas that rise above the Venusian plains and have neutral names.

Mars has several large surface features. Olympus Mons is the largest volcano in the Solar System. It, along with three smaller volcanoes, are located in the Tharsis region. To the east is Valles Marineris a huge 2,500- to 3,000-mile-long canyon discovered by the Mariner 9 spacecraft in the early 1970s. Hellas Planitia and Utopia Planitia are two large lowlands.Of course, we can’t forget the so-called “faces on Mars.”

![Image 6](https://i0.wp.com/www.fas37.org/wp/wp-content/uploads/2025/05/PIA01141_modest.jpeg?ssl=1)

![Image 7](https://i0.wp.com/www.fas37.org/wp/wp-content/uploads/2025/05/face_E03-00824_proc-1024x1024.gif?ssl=1)

![Image 8](https://i0.wp.com/www.fas37.org/wp/wp-content/uploads/2025/05/happy_face-681x1024.jpeg?ssl=1)

“Faces on Mars.” Images Credit: NASA/JPL/Malin Space Science Systems.

Ceres has a couple interesting features that were discovered by the Dawn spacecraft back in 2015. There are two white spots that astronomers think might be composed of salt. Officially they are Cerealia facula and Vinalia facula located within the Occator Crater. There is also an interesting looking mountain called Ahuna Mons.

[![Image 9](https://i0.wp.com/www.fas37.org/wp/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/PIA21906-2-Ceres.jpeg?ssl=1)](https://i0.wp.com/www.fas37.org/wp/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/PIA21906-2-Ceres.jpeg?ssl=1)

Ceres. Image Credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech/UCLA/MPS/DLR/IDA

[![Image 10](https://i0.wp.com/www.fas37.org/wp/wp-content/uploads/2020/10/PIA20355_hires-Occator-Crater.jpg?resize=1024%2C522&ssl=1)](https://i0.wp.com/www.fas37.org/wp/wp-content/uploads/2020/10/PIA20355_hires-Occator-Crater.jpg?ssl=1)

Occator Crater  
Image credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech/UCLA/MPS/DLR/IDA/PSI/LPI

[![Image 11](https://i0.wp.com/www.fas37.org/wp/wp-content/uploads/2020/10/PIA20915_modest-Ahuna-Mons.jpg?resize=769%2C433&ssl=1)](https://i0.wp.com/www.fas37.org/wp/wp-content/uploads/2020/10/PIA20915_modest-Ahuna-Mons.jpg?ssl=1)

Ahuna Mons  
Image Credit:   
NASA/JPL-Caltech/UCLA/MPS/DLR/IDA

Saturn’s largest moon Titan is covered by a thick hazy atmosphere. However, if we can peer through the atmosphere, we find a surface composed of rock-hard water ice along with rolling dunes. There are also seas filled with liquid methane at Titan’s northern pole (Kraken, Ligeia, and Punga Mare). A smaller lake, Ontario Lacus, is found at the southern pole. Two large areas are situated along Titan’s equator. Shangri-La is a dark-colored lowland filled with flowing dunes. Xanadu is a light-colored plateau of ice with mounds and knolls extending above the ground (hummocky).

[![Image 12](https://i0.wp.com/www.fas37.org/wp/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/Titan_comp_ISSimage-pdf.jpg?resize=1024%2C683&ssl=1)](https://www.fas37.org/wp/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/Titan_comp_ISSimage.pdf)

Image Credit: NASA/JPL/Space Science Institute & USGA/IAU/NASA Gazetteer of Planetary Nomenclature

The most noticeable feature on Pluto’s surface is a heart shaped area that is filled with frozen nitrogen. Officially it is Tombaugh Regio (named after Pluto’s discoverer Clyde Tombaugh). The western portion is called Sputnik Planitia (named after the first artificial satellite). Another is a dark area filled with Tholins (organic gunk). It was initially (and unofficially) named Cthulhu Regio but is now officially Belton Regio (after astronomer Michael Belton).

[![Image 13](https://i0.wp.com/www.fas37.org/wp/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/jpegPIA19863.width-1600.jpeg?resize=1024%2C512&ssl=1)](https://i0.wp.com/www.fas37.org/wp/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/jpegPIA19863.width-1600.jpeg?ssl=1)

Image Credit: NASA/Johns Hopkins University Applied Physics Laboratory/  
Southwest Research Institute

[![Image 14](https://i0.wp.com/www.fas37.org/wp/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/pluto-pdf.jpg?resize=1024%2C531&ssl=1)](https://www.fas37.org/wp/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/pluto.pdf)

Image Credit: NASA/Johns Hopkins University Applied Physics Laboratory/  
Southwest Research Institute & USGA/IAU/NASA Gazetteer of Planetary Nomenclature

Many of the surface features on Charon were unofficially named after science fiction references. These included Kirk, Spock, Sulu, and Uhura craters as well as Tardis Chasma and Gallifrey Macula. A dark area, filled with Tholins that carried over from Pluto, was initially referred to as Mordor Macula. However, most of these names have yet to be officially adopted and surface features now have more acceptable (mundane?) names.

### Abstract

The automatic identification of planetary feature names in astronomy publications presents numerous challenges. These features include craters, defined as roughly circular depressions resulting from impact or volcanic activity; dorsas, which are elongate raised structures or wrinkle ridges; and lacus, small irregular patches of dark, smooth material on the Moon, referred to as "lake" (Planetary Names Working Group, n.d.). Many feature names overlap with places or people's names that they are named after, for example, Syria, Tempe, Einstein, and Sagan, to name a few (U.S. Geological Survey, n.d.). Some feature names have been used in many contexts, for instance, Apollo, which can refer to mission, program, sample, astronaut, seismic, seismometers, core, era, data, collection, instrument, and station, in addition to the crater on the Moon. Some feature names can appear in the text as adjectives, like the lunar craters Black, Green, and White. Some feature names in other contexts serve as directions, like craters West and South on the Moon. Additionally, some features share identical names across different celestial bodies, requiring disambiguation, such as the Adams crater, which exists on both the Moon and Mars. We present a multi-step pipeline combining rule-based filtering, statistical relevance analysis, part-of-speech (POS) tagging, named entity recognition (NER) model, hybrid keyword harvesting, knowledge graph (KG) matching, and inference with a locally installed large language model (LLM) to reliably identify planetary names despite these challenges. When evaluated on a dataset of astronomy papers from the Astrophysics Data System (ADS), this methodology achieves an F1-score over 0.97 in disambiguating planetary feature names.

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

The **naming of moons** has been the responsibility of the [International Astronomical Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Astronomical_Union "International Astronomical Union")'s committee for Planetary System Nomenclature since 1973. That committee is known today as the [Working Group for Planetary System Nomenclature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Planetary_nomenclature "Planetary nomenclature") (WGPSN).

Prior to its formation, the names of [satellites](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_satellite "Natural satellite") have had varying histories. The choice of names is often determined by a satellite's discoverer; however, historically some satellites were not given names for many years after their discovery; for instance, [Titan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Titan_(moon) "Titan (moon)") was discovered by [Huygens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christiaan_Huygens "Christiaan Huygens") in 1655, but was not named until 1847, almost two centuries later.

Before the IAU assumed responsibility for astronomical nomenclature, only twenty-five satellites had been given names that were in wide use and are still used: 1 of Earth, 2 of Mars, 5 of Jupiter, 10 of Saturn, 5 of Uranus, and 2 of Neptune.[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naming_of_moons#cite_note-MoonNames-1) Since then, names have been given to 150 additional planetary and dwarf planetary satellites: 52 satellites of [Jupiter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jupiter "Jupiter"), 53 of [Saturn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturn "Saturn"), 22 of [Uranus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uranus "Uranus"), 12 of [Neptune](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neptune "Neptune"), 5 of [Pluto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pluto "Pluto"), 2 of [Haumea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haumea_(dwarf_planet) "Haumea (dwarf planet)"), and 1 each of [Eris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eris_(dwarf_planet) "Eris (dwarf planet)"), [Gonggong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gonggong_(dwarf_planet) "Gonggong (dwarf planet)"), [Quaoar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quaoar "Quaoar"), and [Orcus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orcus_(dwarf_planet) "Orcus (dwarf planet)"). Names have also been given to some satellites of minor planets, including the dwarf planet candidates [Salacia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/120347_Salacia "120347 Salacia") and [Varda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/174567_Varda "174567 Varda") which have one satellite each. The number will continue to rise as current satellite discoveries are documented and new satellites are discovered.

At the IAU General Assembly in July 2004,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naming_of_moons#cite_note-iau.org-2) the WGPSN suggested it may become advisable to not name small satellites, as [CCD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charge-coupled_device "Charge-coupled device") technology makes it possible to discover satellites as small as 1 km in diameter. Until 2014, names were applied to all planetary moons discovered, regardless of size. From 2015, some small moons have not received names.

## Naming of moons by Solar System object

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Naming_of_moons&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Naming of moons by Solar System object")]

### Earth

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Naming_of_moons&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Earth")]

Main article: [Moon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moon "Moon")

Every human language has its own word for the Earth's [Moon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moon "Moon"), and these words are the ones normally used in astronomical contexts. However, a number of fanciful or mythological names for the Moon have been used in the context of astronomy (an even larger number of lunar epithets have been used in non-astronomical contexts). In the 17th century, the Moon was sometimes referred to as _Proserpina_. More recently, especially in science-fiction content, the Moon has been called _Earth I_, analogue to the numbering of Jovian moonswith roman numbers, or by the [Latin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin "Latin") name _Luna_, presumably on the analogy of the Latin names of the planets, or by association with the adjectival form _lunar_, or a need to differentiate it from other moons that may be present in a fictional setting; however, in several Romance languages, such as Spanish, the word "luna" is often used to refer to any natural satellite in the same way as "moon" in English, which is problematic.

In technical terminology, the word-stems _seleno-_ (from [Greek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greek_language "Greek language")_selēnē_ "moon") and _cynthi-_ (from _Cynthia_, an epithet of the goddess [Artemis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artemis "Artemis") or [Diana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diana_(mythology) "Diana (mythology)")) are sometimes used to refer to the Moon, as in _[selenography](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Selenography "Selenography")_, _[selenology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Selenology "Selenology"),_ and _[pericynthion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pericynthion "Pericynthion")_.

### Mars

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Naming_of_moons&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Mars")]

Main article: [Moons of Mars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moons_of_Mars "Moons of Mars")

The moons of [Mars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mars "Mars") ([Phobos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phobos_(moon) "Phobos (moon)") and [Deimos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deimos_(moon) "Deimos (moon)")) were named by [Asaph Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asaph_Hall "Asaph Hall") in 1878, soon after he discovered them. They are named after the sons of the god [Ares](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ares "Ares") (the Greek equivalent of the Roman god [Mars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mars_(mythology) "Mars (mythology)")).

### Jupiter

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Naming_of_moons&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Jupiter")]

Main article: [Moons of Jupiter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moons_of_Jupiter "Moons of Jupiter")

The [Galilean moons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galilean_moons "Galilean moons") of Jupiter ([Io](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Io_(moon) "Io (moon)"), [Europa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Europa_(moon) "Europa (moon)"), [Ganymede](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ganymede_(moon) "Ganymede (moon)") and [Callisto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Callisto_(moon) "Callisto (moon)")) were named by [Simon Marius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_Marius "Simon Marius") soon after their discovery in 1610. However, by the late 19th century these names had fallen out of favor, and for a long time it was most common to refer to them in the astronomical literature simply as "Jupiter I", "Jupiter II", etc., or as "the first satellite of Jupiter", "Jupiter's second satellite", etc.

By the first decade of the 20th century, the names Io, Europa, Ganymede, and Callisto had once again recovered popularity, but the later-discovered moons, numbered, usually in Roman numerals V (5) through XII (12), remained unnamed.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naming_of_moons#cite_note-Nicholson-3)[_[dubious](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Accuracy\_dispute#Disputed\_statement "Wikipedia:Accuracy dispute")–[discuss](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talk:Naming\_of\_moons#source\_is\_from\_1939,\_predates\_XII\_discovery,\_and\_states\_the\_opposite:\_names\_for\_the\_Galilean\_moons\_were\_NOT\_in\_common\_use "Talk:Naming of moons")_] By a popular though unofficial convention,[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] Jupiter V, discovered in 1892, was given the name _Amalthea_,[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naming_of_moons#cite_note-Barnard-4) first used by the French astronomer [Camille Flammarion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Camille_Flammarion "Camille Flammarion").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naming_of_moons#cite_note-5)

The other [irregular satellites](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irregular_satellite "Irregular satellite") (discovered 1904 to 1951) were, in the overwhelming majority of astronomical literature, simply left nameless. No names were proposed until [Brian G. Marsden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_G._Marsden "Brian G. Marsden") suggested a nomenclature for these satellites in 1955.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naming_of_moons#cite_note-Marsden-6) Although the 1955 names met with immediate acceptance in some quarters (e.g. in science fiction[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naming_of_moons#cite_note-Starr-7) and popular science articles[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naming_of_moons#cite_note-Rollcall-8)), they were still rarely if ever met in astronomical literature until the 1970s.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naming_of_moons#cite_note-Gaposchkin-9)

Two other proposals for naming the satellites were made between 1955 and 1975, both by Soviet astronomers, E. I. Nesterovich (in 1962) and Yu. A. Karpenko (in 1973).[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naming_of_moons#cite_note-Owen-10)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naming_of_moons#cite_note-Karpenko-11) These met no particularly enthusiastic reception.

In 1975, following [Charles Kowal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Kowal "Charles Kowal")'s discovery of the satellite Jupiter XIII in 1974, the [IAU](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Astronomical_Union "International Astronomical Union") Task Group for Outer Solar System Nomenclature granted names to satellites V-XIII, and provided for a formal naming process for future satellites to be discovered. Under the new process, Jupiter V continued as [Amalthea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amalthea_(moon) "Amalthea (moon)"), Jupiter XIII was named [Leda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leda_(moon) "Leda (moon)") in accordance with a suggestion of Kowal's, and all previous proposals for the seven satellites VI-XII were abandoned in favor of new names, in accordance with a scheme suggested by the German philologist [Jürgen Blunck](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J%C3%BCrgen_Blunck?action=edit&redlink=1 "Jürgen Blunck (page does not exist)") where [prograde](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Direct_motion "Direct motion") moons received names ending in 'a' and [retrograde](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Retrograde_motion "Retrograde motion") moons received names ending in 'e'.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naming_of_moons#cite_note-12)

The new names met considerable protest from some quarters. Kowal, despite suggesting a name for Jupiter XIII, was of the opinion that Jupiter's irregular satellites should not be named at all.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naming_of_moons#cite_note-Kowal-13)[Carl Sagan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Sagan "Carl Sagan") noted that the names chosen were extraordinarily obscure (a fact that [Tobias Owen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tobias_Owen,_Sr.?action=edit&redlink=1 "Tobias Owen, Sr. (page does not exist)"), chair of the Task Group, admitted was intentional in a response to Sagan[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naming_of_moons#cite_note-Owen-10)) and suggested his own names in 1976;[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naming_of_moons#cite_note-Sagan-14) these preserved some of the names from the 1955 proposal. Karpenko had noted the same in his 1981 book "The Names of the Starry Sky", along with stating that the names chosen for retrograde moons, and therefore the "e" ending, were not always the ones for which it was the more common one.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naming_of_moons#cite_note-15)

The proposals are summarized in the table below (data from _Icarus_ unless specified otherwise[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naming_of_moons#cite_note-Owen-10)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naming_of_moons#cite_note-Sagan-14)):

### Saturn

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Naming_of_moons&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Saturn")]

Main article: [Moons of Saturn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moons_of_Saturn "Moons of Saturn")

In 1847, the seven then known moons of [Saturn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturn "Saturn") were named by [John Herschel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Herschel "John Herschel"). Herschel named Saturn's two innermost moons (Mimas and Enceladus) after the mythological Greek [Giants](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gigantes "Gigantes"), and the outer five after the [Titans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Titan_(mythology) "Titan (mythology)") (Titan, Iapetus) and Titanesses (Tethys, Dione, Rhea) of the same mythology. Until then, [Titan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Titan_(moon) "Titan (moon)") was known as the "Huygenian (or Huyghenian) satellite of Saturn" and the other moons had Roman numeral designations in order of their distance from Saturn. Subsequent discoverers of Saturnian moons followed Herschel's scheme: [Hyperion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyperion_(moon) "Hyperion (moon)") was discovered soon after in 1848, and the ninth moon, [Phoebe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phoebe_(moon) "Phoebe (moon)"), was named by its discoverer in 1899 soon after its discovery; they were named for a Titan and a Titaness respectively. The name of [Janus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Janus_(moon) "Janus (moon)") was suggested by its discoverer, [Audouin Dollfus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Audouin_Dollfus "Audouin Dollfus").

Current IAU practice for newly discovered inner moons is to continue with Herschel's system, naming them after Titans or their descendants. However, the increasing number of moons that were being discovered in the 21st century caused the IAU to draw up a new scheme for the outer moons. At the IAU General Assembly in July 2004,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naming_of_moons#cite_note-iau.org-2) the WGPSN allowed satellites of Saturn to have names of giants and monsters in mythologies other than the Greco-Roman. Since the outer moons fall naturally into three groups, one group is named after [Norse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norse_mythology "Norse mythology") giants, one after [Gallic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celtic_mythology "Celtic mythology") giants, and one after [Inuit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inuit_mythology "Inuit mythology") giants. The only moon that fails to fit this scheme is the Greek-named Phoebe, which is in the Norse group.

### Uranus

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Naming_of_moons&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Uranus")]

Main article: [Moons of Uranus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moons_of_Uranus "Moons of Uranus")

The Roman numbering scheme of [Uranus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uranus "Uranus")' moons was in a state of flux for a considerable time. Sir William Herschel thought he had discovered up to six moons and maybe even a ring. For nearly fifty years, Herschel's instrument was the only one the moons had been seen with.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naming_of_moons#cite_note-17) In the 1840s, better instruments and a more favourable position of Uranus in the sky led to sporadic indications of satellites additional to Titania and Oberon. Publications hesitated between William Herschel's designations (where Titania and Oberon are Uranus II and IV) and William Lassell's (where they are sometimes I and II).[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naming_of_moons#cite_note-18) With the confirmation of Ariel and Umbriel, Lassell numbered the moons I through IV from Uranus outward, and this finally stuck.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naming_of_moons#cite_note-19)

The first two Uranian moons, discovered in 1787, did not receive names until 1852, a year after two more moons had been discovered. The responsibility for naming was taken by [John Herschel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Herschel "John Herschel"), son of the discoverer of Uranus. Herschel, instead of assigning names from [Greek mythology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greek_mythology "Greek mythology"), named the moons after magical spirits in [English literature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_literature "English literature"): the fairies [Oberon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oberon "Oberon") and [Titania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Titania_(A_Midsummer_Night's_Dream) "Titania (A Midsummer Night's Dream)") from [William Shakespeare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Shakespeare "William Shakespeare")'s _[A Midsummer Night's Dream](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A\_Midsummer\_Night's\_Dream "A Midsummer Night's Dream")_, and the sylphs Ariel and Umbriel from [Alexander Pope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Pope "Alexander Pope")'s _[The Rape of the Lock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Rape\_of\_the\_Lock "The Rape of the Lock")_ ([Ariel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ariel_(The_Tempest) "Ariel (The Tempest)") is also a sprite in Shakespeare's _[The Tempest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Tempest "The Tempest")_). The reasoning was presumably that Uranus, as god of the sky and air, would be attended by spirits of the air.

Subsequent names, rather than continuing the "airy spirits" theme (only [Puck](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Puck_(moon) "Puck (moon)") and [Mab](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mab_(moon) "Mab (moon)") continuing the trend), have focused on Herschel's source material. In 1949, the fifth moon, [Miranda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miranda_(moon) "Miranda (moon)"), was named by its discoverer, [Gerard Kuiper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gerard_Kuiper "Gerard Kuiper"), after a thoroughly mortal character in Shakespeare's _[The Tempest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Tempest\_(play) "The Tempest (play)")_. Current IAU practice is to name moons after characters from Shakespeare's plays and _The Rape of the Lock_ (although at present only Ariel, Umbriel, and Belinda have names drawn from the latter poem, all the rest being from Shakespeare). All the retrograde irregular moons are named after characters from one play, _The Tempest_; the only prograde irregular moon, [Margaret](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Margaret_(moon) "Margaret (moon)"), is named from _[Much Ado About Nothing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Much\_Ado\_About\_Nothing "Much Ado About Nothing")_.

### Neptune

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Naming_of_moons&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Neptune")]

Main article: [Moons of Neptune](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moons_of_Neptune "Moons of Neptune")

The one known moon (at the time) of [Neptune](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neptune "Neptune") was not named for many decades. Although the name [Triton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triton_(moon) "Triton (moon)") was suggested in 1880 by [Camille Flammarion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Camille_Flammarion "Camille Flammarion"), it did not come into general use until the mid 20th-century, and for many years was considered "unofficial". In the astronomical literature it was simply referred to as "the satellite of Neptune". Later, the second known moon, [Nereid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nereid_(moon) "Nereid (moon)"), was named by its discoverer in 1949, [Gerard P. Kuiper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gerard_P._Kuiper "Gerard P. Kuiper"), soon after its discovery.

Current IAU practice for newly discovered Neptunian moons is to accord with these first two choices by naming them after Greek sea deities.

For the "normal" irregular satellites, the general convention is to use names ending in "a" for prograde satellites, names ending in "e" for retrograde satellites, and names ending in "o" for exceptionally inclined satellites, exactly like the convention for the [moons of Jupiter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moons_of_Jupiter "Moons of Jupiter").[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naming_of_moons#cite_note-20)

### Pluto

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Naming_of_moons&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Pluto")]

[![Image 4](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d6/Pluto_and_its_five_moons.jpg/250px-Pluto_and_its_five_moons.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Pluto_and_its_five_moons.jpg)

Pluto and its five moons.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naming_of_moons#cite_note-21)

Main article: [Moons of Pluto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moons_of_Pluto "Moons of Pluto")

The name of [Pluto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pluto "Pluto")'s moon [Charon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charon_(moon) "Charon (moon)") was suggested by [James W. Christy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_W._Christy "James W. Christy"), its discoverer, soon after its discovery.

The other four moons are named [Hydra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydra_(moon) "Hydra (moon)"), [Nix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nix_(moon) "Nix (moon)"), [Kerberos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kerberos_(moon) "Kerberos (moon)"), and [Styx](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Styx_(moon) "Styx (moon)").

Charon, Hydra, Nix, and Kerberos are all characters in Greek mythology, with ties to Hades (the Greek equivalent of Pluto). [Charon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charon "Charon") ferries the dead across the River Acheron, [Hydra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lernaean_Hydra "Lernaean Hydra") guards the waters of the underworld, Nix (a respelling of [Nyx](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nyx_(mythology) "Nyx (mythology)")) is the mother of Charon and the goddess of darkness and the night, and Kerberos (a respelling of [Cerberus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cerberus "Cerberus")) is a giant three-headed dog who guards the entrance to the underworld. The fifth moon is named for the river [Styx](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Styx "Styx") that forms the boundary between the worlds of the living and the dead.

### Eris

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Naming_of_moons&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Eris")]

Main article: [Dysnomia (moon)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dysnomia_(moon) "Dysnomia (moon)")

The name of [Eris's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/136199_Eris "136199 Eris") moon [Dysnomia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dysnomia_(moon) "Dysnomia (moon)") was suggested by its discoverer [Michael E. Brown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_E._Brown "Michael E. Brown"), who also suggested the name of the dwarf planet. The name has two meanings: in mythology [Dysnomia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dysnomia_(mythology) "Dysnomia (mythology)") (lawlessness) is the daughter of [Eris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eris_(mythology) "Eris (mythology)") (chaos). However, the name is also an intentional reference to the actor [Lucy Lawless](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucy_Lawless "Lucy Lawless") who plays the character [Xena](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xena:_Warrior_Princess "Xena: Warrior Princess"). The background for this is that during the long period when Eris had no formal name, the name 'Xena' – originally Brown's nickname for his discovery – spread and became popular. When the name 'Eris' was chosen, Brown suggested Dysnomia (which until then had been referred to as [Gabrielle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gabrielle_(Xena) "Gabrielle (Xena)")) as a reference to this.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naming_of_moons#cite_note-22) Hence, Dysnomia is the only moon which could be said to be named after an actor. The names Eris and Dysnomia were accepted by the IAU on 14 September 2006.

### Orcus

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Naming_of_moons&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Orcus")]

Main article: [Vanth (moon)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vanth_(moon) "Vanth (moon)")

On 23 March 2009, Brown asked readers of his weekly column to suggest possible names for the satellite of Orcus which he had codiscovered, with the best one to be submitted to the [International Astronomical Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Astronomical_Union "International Astronomical Union") (IAU) on 5 April.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naming_of_moons#cite_note-MBP-26) The name [Vanth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vanth "Vanth"), the winged [Etruscan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Etruscan_mythology "Etruscan mythology")[psychopomp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psychopomp "Psychopomp") who guides the souls of the dead to the underworld, was chosen from among a large pool of submissions. Vanth was the only suggestion that was purely Etruscan in origin. It was the most popular submission, first suggested by [Sonya Taaffe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sonya_Taaffe "Sonya Taaffe").[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naming_of_moons#cite_note-brown16-27)

The Etruscan Vanth is frequently portrayed in the company of [Charun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charun "Charun") (Charon), and so as the name of the moon of Orcus (nicknamed the "anti-Pluto" because resonance with Neptune keeps it on the opposite side of the Sun from Pluto), it is an allusion to the parallels between Orcus and [Pluto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pluto "Pluto"). Brown quoted Taaffe as saying that if Vanth "accompanies dead souls from the moment of death to the underworld itself, then of course her face is turned always toward Orcus", a reference to the likely synchronous orbit of Vanth about Orcus.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naming_of_moons#cite_note-brown16-27)

## Roman numeral designations

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Naming_of_moons&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section:  Roman numeral designations")]

The Roman numbering system for satellites arose with the very first discovery of natural satellites other than Earth's Moon: [Galileo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galileo "Galileo") referred to the [Galilean moons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galilean_moons "Galilean moons") as **I** through **IV** (counting from Jupiter outward), refusing to adopt the names proposed by his rival [Simon Marius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_Marius "Simon Marius"). Similar numbering schemes naturally arose with the discovery of multiple moons around Saturn, Uranus, and Mars. The numbers initially designated the moons in orbital sequence, and were re-numbered after each new discovery; for instance, before the discovery of Mimas and Enceladus in 1789, Tethys was Saturn I, Dione Saturn II, etc.,[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naming_of_moons#cite_note-28) but after the new moons were discovered, Mimas became Saturn I, Enceladus Saturn II, Tethys Saturn III and Dione Saturn IV.

In the middle of the 19th century, however, the numeration became fixed, and later discoveries failed to conform with the orbital sequence scheme. [Amalthea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amalthea_(moon) "Amalthea (moon)"), discovered in 1892, was labelled "Jupiter V" although it orbits more closely to Jupiter than does [Io](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Io_(moon) "Io (moon)") (Jupiter I). The unstated convention then became, at the close of the 19th century, that the numbers more or less reflected the order of discovery, except for prior historical exceptions (see [Timeline of discovery of Solar System planets and their natural satellites](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_discovery_of_Solar_System_planets_and_their_natural_satellites "Timeline of discovery of Solar System planets and their natural satellites")); though if a large number of satellites were discovered in a short span of time, the group could be numbered in orbital sequence, or according to other principles than strictly by order of discovery. The convention has been extended to natural satellites of minor planets, such as [(87) Sylvia I Romulus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/(87)_Sylvia_I_Romulus "(87) Sylvia I Romulus"). The outer irregular satellites of Jupiter (VI through XII) were left officially unnamed throughout this period, although as stated above some unofficial names were used in some contexts.

From 1975 to 2009, the [International Astronomical Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Astronomical_Union "International Astronomical Union") was assigning names to all planetary satellites, and Roman numerals were usually not assigned to satellites until they are named. (An exception is Saturn's moon [Helene](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helene_(moon) "Helene (moon)"), which received the Roman numeral XII in 1982, but was not named until 1988.) During this period, the use of Roman numeral designations diminished, and some are very rarely used; [Phobos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phobos_(moon) "Phobos (moon)") and [Deimos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deimos_(moon) "Deimos (moon)") are rarely referred to as Mars I and Mars II, and the [Moon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moon "Moon") is never referred to as "Earth I". However, since 2015 some moons have again been numbered without being named, starting from [Jupiter LI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jupiter_LI "Jupiter LI").

The thirteen named satellites of Saturn from [Aegir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aegir_(moon) "Aegir (moon)") to [Surtur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surtur_(moon) "Surtur (moon)") were named in [alphabetical order](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alphabetical_order "Alphabetical order") corresponding to their Roman numerals.

## Provisional designations

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Naming_of_moons&action=edit&section=16 "Edit section: Provisional designations")]

Further information: [Provisional designation in astronomy §Satellites and rings of planets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Provisional_designation_in_astronomy#Satellites_and_rings_of_planets "Provisional designation in astronomy")

When satellites are first discovered, they are given provisional designations such as "[S/2010 J 2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jupiter_LII "Jupiter LII")" (the 2nd new satellite of Jupiter discovered in 2010) or "[S/2003 S 1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/S/2003_S_1 "S/2003 S 1")" (the 1st new satellite of Saturn discovered in 2003). The initial "S/" stands for "satellite", and distinguishes from such prefixes as "D/", "C/", and "P/", used for [comets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comet "Comet"). The designation "R/" is used for planetary rings. These designations are sometimes written like "S/2003 S1", dropping the second space. The letter following the category and year identifies the planet (**J**upiter, **S**aturn, **U**ranus, **N**eptune; although no occurrence of the other planets is expected, Mars and Mercury are disambiguated through the use of **H**ermes for the latter). [Pluto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pluto "Pluto") was designated by **P** prior to its [recategorization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IAU_definition_of_planet "IAU definition of planet") as a [dwarf planet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dwarf_planet "Dwarf planet"). When the object is found around a minor planet, the identifier used is the latter's number in parentheses. Thus, [Dactyl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dactyl_(asteroid) "Dactyl (asteroid)"), the moon of [243 Ida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/243_Ida "243 Ida"), was at first designated "[S/1993 (243) 1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/S/1993_(243)_1 "S/1993 (243) 1")". Once confirmed and named, it became **[(243) Ida I Dactyl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/(243)_Ida_I_Dactyl "(243) Ida I Dactyl")**. Similarly, the fourth satellite of Pluto, [Kerberos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kerberos_(moon) "Kerberos (moon)"), discovered after Pluto was categorized as a dwarf planet and assigned a minor planet number, was designated [S/2011 (134340) 1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/S/2011_(134340)_1 "S/2011 (134340) 1") rather than S/2011 P 1,[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naming_of_moons#cite_note-29) though the _[New Horizons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New\_Horizons "New Horizons")_ team, who maintained that dwarf planets were planets, used the latter.

*   **H** = [Mercury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercury_(planet) "Mercury (planet)") (Hermes)
*   **V** = [Venus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venus "Venus")
*   **E** = [Earth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth "Earth")
*   **M** = [Mars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mars "Mars")
*   **J** = [Jupiter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jupiter "Jupiter")
*   **S** = [Saturn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturn "Saturn")
*   **U** = [Uranus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uranus "Uranus")
*   **N** = [Neptune](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neptune "Neptune")

Note: The assignation of "H" for Mercury is specified by the [USGS Gazetteer of Planetary Nomenclature](https://web.archive.org/web/20071002230241/http://planetarynames.wr.usgs.gov/specifics.html); since they usually follow IAU guidelines closely, this is very likely the IAU convention, but confirmation is needed: there have been no moons found to be orbiting Mercury as of yet.

After a few months or years, when a newly discovered satellite's existence has been confirmed and its orbit computed, a permanent name is chosen, which replaces the "S/" provisional designation. However, in the past, some satellites remained unnamed for surprisingly long periods after their discovery.

## Timeline

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Naming_of_moons&action=edit&section=17 "Edit section: Timeline")]

The timeline only includes moons of the planets and the more likely dwarf planets. [Ceres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ceres_(dwarf_planet) "Ceres (dwarf planet)") (no moons), [Orcus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orcus_(dwarf_planet) "Orcus (dwarf planet)"), [Pluto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pluto "Pluto"), [Haumea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haumea "Haumea"), [Quaoar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quaoar "Quaoar"), [Makemake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Makemake "Makemake") (unnamed moon), [Gonggong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gonggong_(dwarf_planet) "Gonggong (dwarf planet)"), [Eris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eris_(dwarf_planet) "Eris (dwarf planet)"), and [Sedna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sedna_(dwarf_planet) "Sedna (dwarf planet)") (no moons) are generally agreed among astronomers to be dwarf planets. [Salacia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/120347_Salacia "120347 Salacia") and [Varda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/174567_Varda "174567 Varda") are more controversial.

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

The **naming of moons** has been the responsibility of the [International Astronomical Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Astronomical_Union "International Astronomical Union")'s committee for Planetary System Nomenclature since 1973. That committee is known today as the [Working Group for Planetary System Nomenclature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Planetary_nomenclature "Planetary nomenclature") (WGPSN).

Prior to its formation, the names of [satellites](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_satellite "Natural satellite") have had varying histories. The choice of names is often determined by a satellite's discoverer; however, historically some satellites were not given names for many years after their discovery; for instance, [Titan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Titan_(moon) "Titan (moon)") was discovered by [Huygens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christiaan_Huygens "Christiaan Huygens") in 1655, but was not named until 1847, almost two centuries later.

Before the IAU assumed responsibility for astronomical nomenclature, only twenty-five satellites had been given names that were in wide use and are still used: 1 of Earth, 2 of Mars, 5 of Jupiter, 10 of Saturn, 5 of Uranus, and 2 of Neptune.[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naming_of_moons#cite_note-MoonNames-1) Since then, names have been given to 150 additional planetary and dwarf planetary satellites: 52 satellites of [Jupiter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jupiter "Jupiter"), 53 of [Saturn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturn "Saturn"), 22 of [Uranus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uranus "Uranus"), 12 of [Neptune](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neptune "Neptune"), 5 of [Pluto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pluto "Pluto"), 2 of [Haumea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haumea_(dwarf_planet) "Haumea (dwarf planet)"), and 1 each of [Eris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eris_(dwarf_planet) "Eris (dwarf planet)"), [Gonggong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gonggong_(dwarf_planet) "Gonggong (dwarf planet)"), [Quaoar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quaoar "Quaoar"), and [Orcus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orcus_(dwarf_planet) "Orcus (dwarf planet)"). Names have also been given to some satellites of minor planets, including the dwarf planet candidates [Salacia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/120347_Salacia "120347 Salacia") and [Varda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/174567_Varda "174567 Varda") which have one satellite each. The number will continue to rise as current satellite discoveries are documented and new satellites are discovered.

At the IAU General Assembly in July 2004,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naming_of_moons#cite_note-iau.org-2) the WGPSN suggested it may become advisable to not name small satellites, as [CCD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charge-coupled_device "Charge-coupled device") technology makes it possible to discover satellites as small as 1 km in diameter. Until 2014, names were applied to all planetary moons discovered, regardless of size. From 2015, some small moons have not received names.

## Naming of moons by Solar System object

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Naming_of_moons&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Naming of moons by Solar System object")]

### Earth

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Naming_of_moons&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Earth")]

Main article: [Moon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moon "Moon")

Every human language has its own word for the Earth's [Moon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moon "Moon"), and these words are the ones normally used in astronomical contexts. However, a number of fanciful or mythological names for the Moon have been used in the context of astronomy (an even larger number of lunar epithets have been used in non-astronomical contexts). In the 17th century, the Moon was sometimes referred to as _Proserpina_. More recently, especially in science-fiction content, the Moon has been called _Earth I_, analogue to the numbering of Jovian moonswith roman numbers, or by the [Latin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin "Latin") name _Luna_, presumably on the analogy of the Latin names of the planets, or by association with the adjectival form _lunar_, or a need to differentiate it from other moons that may be present in a fictional setting; however, in several Romance languages, such as Spanish, the word "luna" is often used to refer to any natural satellite in the same way as "moon" in English, which is problematic.

In technical terminology, the word-stems _seleno-_ (from [Greek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greek_language "Greek language")_selēnē_ "moon") and _cynthi-_ (from _Cynthia_, an epithet of the goddess [Artemis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artemis "Artemis") or [Diana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diana_(mythology) "Diana (mythology)")) are sometimes used to refer to the Moon, as in _[selenography](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Selenography "Selenography")_, _[selenology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Selenology "Selenology"),_ and _[pericynthion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pericynthion "Pericynthion")_.

### Mars

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Naming_of_moons&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Mars")]

Main article: [Moons of Mars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moons_of_Mars "Moons of Mars")

The moons of [Mars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mars "Mars") ([Phobos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phobos_(moon) "Phobos (moon)") and [Deimos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deimos_(moon) "Deimos (moon)")) were named by [Asaph Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asaph_Hall "Asaph Hall") in 1878, soon after he discovered them. They are named after the sons of the god [Ares](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ares "Ares") (the Greek equivalent of the Roman god [Mars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mars_(mythology) "Mars (mythology)")).

### Jupiter

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Naming_of_moons&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Jupiter")]

Main article: [Moons of Jupiter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moons_of_Jupiter "Moons of Jupiter")

The [Galilean moons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galilean_moons "Galilean moons") of Jupiter ([Io](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Io_(moon) "Io (moon)"), [Europa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Europa_(moon) "Europa (moon)"), [Ganymede](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ganymede_(moon) "Ganymede (moon)") and [Callisto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Callisto_(moon) "Callisto (moon)")) were named by [Simon Marius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_Marius "Simon Marius") soon after their discovery in 1610. However, by the late 19th century these names had fallen out of favor, and for a long time it was most common to refer to them in the astronomical literature simply as "Jupiter I", "Jupiter II", etc., or as "the first satellite of Jupiter", "Jupiter's second satellite", etc.

By the first decade of the 20th century, the names Io, Europa, Ganymede, and Callisto had once again recovered popularity, but the later-discovered moons, numbered, usually in Roman numerals V (5) through XII (12), remained unnamed.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naming_of_moons#cite_note-Nicholson-3)[_[dubious](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Accuracy\_dispute#Disputed\_statement "Wikipedia:Accuracy dispute")–[discuss](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talk:Naming\_of\_moons#source\_is\_from\_1939,\_predates\_XII\_discovery,\_and\_states\_the\_opposite:\_names\_for\_the\_Galilean\_moons\_were\_NOT\_in\_common\_use "Talk:Naming of moons")_] By a popular though unofficial convention,[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] Jupiter V, discovered in 1892, was given the name _Amalthea_,[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naming_of_moons#cite_note-Barnard-4) first used by the French astronomer [Camille Flammarion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Camille_Flammarion "Camille Flammarion").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naming_of_moons#cite_note-5)

The other [irregular satellites](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irregular_satellite "Irregular satellite") (discovered 1904 to 1951) were, in the overwhelming majority of astronomical literature, simply left nameless. No names were proposed until [Brian G. Marsden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_G._Marsden "Brian G. Marsden") suggested a nomenclature for these satellites in 1955.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naming_of_moons#cite_note-Marsden-6) Although the 1955 names met with immediate acceptance in some quarters (e.g. in science fiction[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naming_of_moons#cite_note-Starr-7) and popular science articles[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naming_of_moons#cite_note-Rollcall-8)), they were still rarely if ever met in astronomical literature until the 1970s.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naming_of_moons#cite_note-Gaposchkin-9)

Two other proposals for naming the satellites were made between 1955 and 1975, both by Soviet astronomers, E. I. Nesterovich (in 1962) and Yu. A. Karpenko (in 1973).[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naming_of_moons#cite_note-Owen-10)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naming_of_moons#cite_note-Karpenko-11) These met no particularly enthusiastic reception.

In 1975, following [Charles Kowal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Kowal "Charles Kowal")'s discovery of the satellite Jupiter XIII in 1974, the [IAU](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Astronomical_Union "International Astronomical Union") Task Group for Outer Solar System Nomenclature granted names to satellites V-XIII, and provided for a formal naming process for future satellites to be discovered. Under the new process, Jupiter V continued as [Amalthea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amalthea_(moon) "Amalthea (moon)"), Jupiter XIII was named [Leda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leda_(moon) "Leda (moon)") in accordance with a suggestion of Kowal's, and all previous proposals for the seven satellites VI-XII were abandoned in favor of new names, in accordance with a scheme suggested by the German philologist [Jürgen Blunck](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J%C3%BCrgen_Blunck?action=edit&redlink=1 "Jürgen Blunck (page does not exist)") where [prograde](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Direct_motion "Direct motion") moons received names ending in 'a' and [retrograde](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Retrograde_motion "Retrograde motion") moons received names ending in 'e'.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naming_of_moons#cite_note-12)

The new names met considerable protest from some quarters. Kowal, despite suggesting a name for Jupiter XIII, was of the opinion that Jupiter's irregular satellites should not be named at all.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naming_of_moons#cite_note-Kowal-13)[Carl Sagan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Sagan "Carl Sagan") noted that the names chosen were extraordinarily obscure (a fact that [Tobias Owen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tobias_Owen,_Sr.?action=edit&redlink=1 "Tobias Owen, Sr. (page does not exist)"), chair of the Task Group, admitted was intentional in a response to Sagan[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naming_of_moons#cite_note-Owen-10)) and suggested his own names in 1976;[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naming_of_moons#cite_note-Sagan-14) these preserved some of the names from the 1955 proposal. Karpenko had noted the same in his 1981 book "The Names of the Starry Sky", along with stating that the names chosen for retrograde moons, and therefore the "e" ending, were not always the ones for which it was the more common one.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naming_of_moons#cite_note-15)
